concepts.name: Anchoring bias
concepts.source_span: Anchoring bias is relying too heavily on the first piece of information we receive.

questions.stem: What is anchoring bias?
options: Continuing something because of past effort
Remembering only information that agrees with us
Judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind
Relying too heavily on the first piece of information we receive

questions.stem: A shirt marked down from 2000 to 1000 rupees seems cheap. Which bias is at work?
How do negotiators use anchoring?
Which of these is an example of anchoring?
options: Reading only news that agrees with you
Judging a price by comparing it with the first, much higher price you saw
Fearing flights after a crash report
Staying in a job because you trained for years

questions.stem: Anchoring bias involves which piece of information?

concepts.name: Confirmation bias
concepts.source_span: Confirmation bias is the tendency to look for, notice and remember information that supports what we already believe.

questions.stem: What is confirmation bias?
options: The tendency to favour information that supports what we already believe
Relying on the first number we hear
Judging by how vivid examples are

questions.stem: Someone who thinks a team is unlucky remembers every loss and forgets the wins. This is:
Why does confirmation bias make it hard to change our minds?
options: Evidence against our view is ignored or dismissed

questions.stem: Confirmation bias affects which information?
options: Only what we hear from friends
What we look for, notice and remember

questions.stem: Which behaviour shows confirmation bias?
options: Changing your opinion after new evidence
Reading only articles that agree with your opinion
Asking an expert for the full picture

concepts.name: Sunk cost fallacy
concepts.source_span: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing something because of the time, money or effort already spent, even when stopping would be better.

questions.stem: What is the sunk cost fallacy?
options: Preferring information that agrees with us
Believing the first price we see
Continuing something because of the time, money or effort already spent

questions.stem: Watching a boring film to the end because you paid for the ticket is an example of:
Why should a past cost not decide the choice?
options: The past cost cannot be recovered
It was a mistake to spend it

questions.stem: What should the choice depend on instead?
Which of these is a sunk cost?
options: The price of a new product
Money already spent on a ticket that cannot be refunded
Money you may earn next month

concepts.name: Availability heuristic
concepts.source_span: The availability heuristic is judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

questions.stem: What is the availability heuristic?
options: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind
Trusting the first piece of information

questions.stem: After news about a plane crash, people think flying is more dangerous than driving. Which idea explains this?
Which events feel more common than they really are?
According to the example, which causes far more deaths?
The availability heuristic is mainly about:

concepts.name: Dunning-Kruger effect
concepts.source_span: The Dunning-Kruger effect is the tendency of people with low skill in an area to overestimate their own ability.

questions.stem: What is the Dunning-Kruger effect?
options: People with low skill tending to overestimate their ability

questions.stem: Why do beginners often overestimate themselves?
options: They do not know enough to see their own mistakes

questions.stem: How can experts differ from beginners here?
options: They can underestimate how much they know compared with others

questions.stem: Which person fits the Dunning-Kruger effect?
options: A new learner who is sure they are excellent after one lesson
A student who asks for feedback

questions.stem: The effect is about:

concepts.name: Framing effect
concepts.source_span: The framing effect is when our choice changes depending on how the same information is presented.

questions.stem: What is the framing effect?
options: When we only see a picture frame
When our choice changes depending on how the same information is presented
When we trust the first price

questions.stem: Which description do people tend to prefer for the same treatment?
In the treatment example, the facts in both descriptions are:
A gain frame and a loss frame feel:
options: Different, even for the same facts

questions.stem: Which sentence is a loss frame?
options: Ninety percent of patients will survive
Ten percent of patients will die
